title: How Finite Capacity Scheduling Actually Works in Manufacturing

quotes.text: Finite capacity scheduling doesn't create capacity. It makes the competition for capacity visible while you still have time to choose.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Sums up the real value of finite scheduling in two sentences.

quotes.text: Late orders are useful information. Nobody likes them obviously. But a late flag from a finite schedule can tell you something a green plan date cannot.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes late flags as early warning rather than failure.

quotes.text: A changeover isn't dead time between two production orders. It's real work that burns the same resource hours that production does.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why setups must be scheduled like production work.

quotes.text: Generative AI should not replace deterministic scheduling logic. It can explain a recommendation and summarize options and it can retrieve current facts from ERP, MES, maintenance and quality data.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Draws a clear boundary for AI in production scheduling.

quotes.text: Good language does not repair missing production context. It only makes the gaps sound more convincing.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A memorable warning about trusting fluent AI answers without data.

takeaways: ERP and MRP plan against infinite capacity, so finite capacity scheduling is needed to test whether work actually fits the usable time of machines, people, tools and material.
Sequencing and changeovers are policy decisions with trade-offs between due dates, setups and downstream flow, and a good schedule makes those consequences visible to the planner.

Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, Power Platform and Copilot support data, exceptions and explanations, but the scheduling logic and plant-specific rules must live in an engine such as an APS system that the plant owns.
hook: Your ERP assigns a finish date, but the machine that must make the parts is already buried under more work than it can finish. This episode explains for manufacturing planners and IT/OT teams how finite capacity scheduling works, from bottlenecks, changeovers and material release to rescheduling, APS and where Microsoft Fabric, Power Platform and Copilot fit.
